Chapter Eight: Navigating Systemic Barriers and Advocating for Change
So, let’s talk about something that goes beyond just personal strategies—how the bigger picture, the systems around us, can shape women’s advancement at work. Sure, your own habits and mindset matter a lot, but sometimes it feels like you’re pushing against invisible walls, doesn’t it?
Think about biases in hiring and promotion, the way opportunities get handed out, or even those subtle cultural expectations about who’s “supposed” to lead. These aren’t just personal hurdles—they’re woven into the fabric of many workplaces.
Navigating these challenges takes a mix of personal resilience and coming together with others. I like to picture the workplace as an ecosystem—your growth depends on the environment, and real, lasting change usually means shifting things at several levels.
So, how do you start tackling these bigger barriers? Here are a few ideas:
First, get curious about the kinds of bias that show up in organizations and how they play out in everyday decisions. The more you know, the better equipped you are to spot them.
Next, use data—real evidence—to shine a light on the gaps you see. When you’re advocating for fairer policies, numbers can make your case much stronger.
Don’t try to do it alone, either. Build alliances with colleagues who care about inclusion and fairness. There’s real power in teaming up.
And get involved—whether that means joining employee resource groups, signing up for mentorship programs, or supporting diversity initiatives. Every bit helps.
Here’s a simple example: maybe you notice the promotion process at your company feels fuzzy, or the rules seem to shift from person to person. Don’t be afraid to gather your observations and bring it up with decision-makers. Try framing the conversation around how clear, fair criteria actually help attract and keep top talent.
Now, let’s be real—pushing for change can be exhausting, both mentally and emotionally. If you find yourself feeling drained, reach out to trusted peers or mentors, or tap into your professional networks. And don’t forget to take care of yourself along the way. Maintaining your own resilience really matters.
When you combine your own actions with collective advocacy, you can help create a workplace that’s more supportive and inclusive—not just for yourself, but for everyone.
That’s how meaningful change gets started.
